title: Flat On Purpose
logline: In dry-zone paddy country a circle of ground about ten metres across is cleared of every weed, pebble and twig, plastered with a slurry of anthill clay and cattle dung, floated smooth, left to dry, cracked overnight in a net of fine lines, filled and floated smooth again, until it is a plain lighter-coloured disc lying in the stubble with absolutely nothing on it and nothing about it worth looking at.
human_question: What can a person do with attention that has been given nowhere interesting to land?

place.what_kind_of_place: Inland dry-zone country a long way behind the coast, in the belt of small village tanks where the scrub gives way to paddy in the low ground and comes back on the high ground. Red-brown earth, tamarind and palu and kumbuk on the bunds, thorn scrub on the rises, gravel roads, hamlets of a few dozen houses, and holdings measured in acres rather than hectares. In the flat ground below a bund, at the edge of the fields it serves, lies the working object: a circle of beaten earth eight to twelve metres across, raised very slightly above the ground around it, with a short post standing at its centre. It is not a building and it is not a yard. It is a made surface, and everything about how it is made is subtraction: weeds cut off with a mammoty without breaking the ground under them, debris swept away with a twig besom, grit and pebbles picked out of the earth by hand, then a thin slurry of clay taken from a termite mound mixed with cattle dung poured on, spread, and worked flat with a wooden float and the heel of a hand. The equipment is a mammoty, a besom, a bucket, a float, water. There is no machine in it, there is nothing to measure it with, and the only test of the surface is a hand run across it and an eye held low along it.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because it is one of the few things people make in order for it to be uninteresting, and because the finished thing is a perfect circle of nothing in the middle of a landscape full of detail. From height at the beginning or end of a day, the country is all texture: stubble in strips, bunds, scrub, water, the shadows of tree lines, and in the middle of it one smooth disc a shade lighter than everything else, holding no shadow at all, reading as a hole cut in the picture. That shot is beautiful before it means anything and it is also the whole concept. At arm's length the film is small precise work with an obvious purpose: a thumb and finger lifting a pebble out of wet clay, a besom going over the same square metre four times, slurry breaking as it is spread, a float going back and forward until the marks it leaves stop showing, a hand laid flat and moved slowly across a surface to find a grain that should not be there. And then the part nobody would invent: the surface dries, cracks in a fine net across its whole face, and the work is done again on the same ground, and again, because a thing made not to change changes anyway.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The making, the cracking and the re-making, on the clock the weather sets. Wet slurry goes on in the cool of a morning and is worked before it stiffens; by the next morning the face has crazed and has to be filled and floated again; a heavy shower puts the whole thing back to the beginning. Then the object's own working life, which is short and is the opposite of the film's subject: paddy comes onto it, is spread, turned, raked and heaped, and the floor is buried in exactly the material it was made to keep clean. At the end it is swept bare again, and what is swept off it is dust, chaff and the grit that got in anyway. Across a longer clock the object itself is going: threshing here was done with cattle walking a circle round the centre post, and machines have taken most of that work, so that the same circle is now often made only to dry a crop on. Whether the floor a crew can film is still made the old way, by hand, with clay and dung, is the single thing the film depends on and cannot assume.
place.when_it_looks_best: The harvest, and inside it the two or three days when a floor is being prepared, which is set by the crop and not by a calendar. A dry, still stretch, because the surface is worked wet in the open. Within a day the first hour and the last, when the disc separates from the stubble and the whole country goes to texture; and deliberately noon, when the shadows go, the circle flattens into the ground and there is nothing in the frame to look at, which is the concept stated by the light rather than by the voice.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about making a surface. Stubble from height at first light with one smooth circle in it; weeds taken off with a mammoty; a twig besom going over the same ground again and again; pebbles picked out by hand and dropped into a tin; clay dug from a termite mound and mixed with dung and water; the slurry poured and spread and floated; the light going and the circle holding no shadow; the next morning's net of cracks, close enough to count; the same slurry pressed into them with a thumb; the float again; a hand laid flat and drawn slowly across a finished face; then paddy spread all over it, raked, heaped, and the floor swept bare again. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it, and anyone who likes dry-zone country, open light, or work whose whole aim is that nothing should show has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same two or three days become the sources' account of how the training in stillness actually starts, which is not with a state of mind but with a piece of craft. The old text describes preparing a plain disc of earth: picking out the pebbles and twigs, kneading and levelling it, and levelling it again when it cracks as it dries, until the surface is as smooth as a drum face, and then attending to it by one plain name and ignoring its colour and its feel. The object is made to give attention nothing to think about. The voice never says the people making this floor are meditating, never says the floor is a meditation object, and never says anybody here has attained anything. It says the sources describe an object made deliberately dull as a support for attention, that they name a threshing floor themselves as a place where the sign can come, that this is one of forty such supports and that not all of them go the same distance, and that the source's own promise for an ordinary person is small.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high and looking down. Harvested strips, bunds, scrub, the far edge of a tank. In the middle of the frame one smooth circle of bare earth, a shade lighter than everything round it, holding no shadow, with a short post at its centre.
sequence.voice: Everything in this frame has something to look at except one thing. The circle was cleared, plastered and smoothed by hand over two days, and the whole point of the work was that when it was finished there would be nothing on it and nothing about it to hold anybody's eye.

sequence.on_screen: Close, at ground level. Weeds cut off with a mammoty without turning the soil. A twig besom going over the same square metre four times. Two fingers lifting a pebble out of the surface and dropping it into a tin. Clay dug out of a termite mound, mixed with dung and water, poured and spread.
sequence.voice: The old manual for this training begins as a piece of craft, and describes it in this order: pick out the pebbles and the twigs, knead the earth, and level it; and when it dries and cracks, level it again, until the surface is as smooth as the face of a drum [C087-P4:L209–L213].

sequence.on_screen: The next morning. The dried face crazed across its whole width in a net of fine cracks, filmed close enough to count them. The same slurry worked into them with a thumb. The float going back and forward until it stops leaving marks. A hand laid flat and drawn slowly across the surface.
sequence.voice: The instruction for what to do with the finished thing is almost rude in how little it asks. Do not attend to its colour. Do not attend to how it feels. Hold one plain word for it and nothing else [C087-P4:L213]. The lay handbook is just as practical about the object itself, and allows a tray, a board, a patch of cement, whatever will hold a plain face [C087-M:L19–L29].

sequence.on_screen: The finished floor, held long and in one shot: empty, level, the post at its centre, the stubble beginning at its edge. Nothing enters the frame. Then the same floor at noon, with the shadows gone and the circle almost indistinguishable from the ground.
sequence.voice: What such an object is for, the sources explain by an ordinary act. Someone who wants to really know a thing brings it close, stops looking anywhere else, and looks for a long time at its colours and its marks until all of it is plain [C013-P:L48–L52]. The disc of earth is the standard thing they have this done to [C013-P:L155]. And the text names a threshing floor itself, in as many words, as a place where somebody with long practice behind them may find the sign at once [C013-P:L133].

sequence.on_screen: The floor in use, and unrecognisable: paddy spread across the whole disc, raked, turned, walked on, heaped. Then the same floor swept bare again at the end of the day, with dust, chaff and grit going off the edge.
sequence.voice: This object is one of forty. The compendium is a list of forty things attention can be brought back to, and it is strict about two of them: the object is supposed to be matched to the temperament of the person using it and taken from somebody who knows, not picked by liking [C085-P:L47]; and the forty do not all go the same distance, because ten of them only ever bring the mind as far as the doorway and never through it [C085-P4:L61].

sequence.on_screen: Late light. The disc from height again, and then a long still frame of its empty surface from a low angle, the grain of the float visible where the light rakes it.
sequence.voice: The sources are careful not to oversell what this kind of work does. They say a settled mind holds wanting, anger, dullness, agitation and doubt down only while it lasts, and they put it like this: dip a pot into a pond and the moss parts, and when the pot comes out the moss drifts back over the same water [C013-P:L62; C013-P:L66].

sequence.on_screen: The tools going back against a wall: mammoty, besom, float, bucket. The tin of picked-out pebbles tipped out at the edge of the field.
sequence.voice: For an ordinary person the promise in the lay handbook is small and exact. Half an hour to an hour a day, kept up for some months, brings some steadiness, a liking for sitting still, and a quieter and more harmless way of living [C087-M:L13; C087-M:L39]. Of the full method it says plainly that it is very hard and suits perhaps one person in tens of thousands [C087-M:L9].

sequence.on_screen: Last light from height, wider than the opening: the disc, the bund, the tank, the scrub, the tree line, and the light going off all of it at once.
sequence.voice: Three things this film is not saying. Nobody in it is meditating, nobody's state of mind is visible to a camera, and no calm anybody here shows is an attainment of anything. The powers the old text lists further on as fruits of this practice are its own claims and are not a promise made to anybody watching [C087-P4:L464–L484]. And the sources themselves refuse the obvious conclusion: settling the mind is the ground, and what they say actually frees is seeing clearly, which is a different piece of work [C085-M:L11].

concept_merge.why_together: C087 carries the film and supplies its object. The digest's opening human reading is literally a craft instruction: pick out the pebbles and twigs, knead and level the earth, and level it again when it cracks as it dries, until the surface is as smooth as a drum face, then sit at a set distance and hold one plain word for it, ignoring its colour and texture [C087-P4:L209–L213; C087-P4:L213]. The lay text allows the object to be built on a tray, a board or a patch of cement [C087-M:L19–L29], is frank that the full monastic method is very hard and suits perhaps one in tens of thousands [C087-M:L9], and offers an ordinary person half an hour to an hour a day for some months in exchange for some steadiness and a quieter life [C087-M:L13; C087-M:L39]. C013 is what turns the object from a curiosity into a reason, because it supplies the sources' own account of why a plain thing looked at for a long time does anything at all: bring it close, stop looking elsewhere, look long at its colours and marks until it is completely clear [C013-P:L48–L52]; it names the earth disc as the standard object [C013-P:L155]; and it names a threshing floor, unprompted, as a place where a practised person may find the sign at once [C013-P:L133], which is the single most useful sentence either digest offers this film. C013 also supplies the film's brake, the moss and the pot, which says that calm holds things down only while it lasts [C013-P:L62; C013-P:L66]. C085 keeps the object in proportion: it is one of forty, it is supposed to be fitted to the person and taken from a teacher rather than chosen by taste [C085-P:L47], the forty have different ceilings and ten of them never pass the doorway [C085-P4:L61], and calm is not what frees [C085-M:L11].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the training the texts describe starts in dirt and repetition, and that its first object is something a person makes on purpose to be worth nothing to the eye. Said flat, 'a meditation object' is an abstraction. Made on screen as a circle of ground cleared of grit, plastered, floated, cracked and floated again, it becomes a job with a standard, and the standard is negative: the surface is finished when there is nothing on it and nothing in it to notice. The film also gets three of the sources' own corrections for nothing. It gets the modesty, because the same afternoon's work is repeated for the third time and nothing has been achieved. It gets the impermanence of calm, because the surface it took two days to perfect will be under a foot of paddy by the weekend and crazed again by the next dry week. And it gets the ceiling, because the object is plainly a support for something else and is not the something else. This idea has been round twice before. Its first version was a clay-worker making training discs to order for a meditation teacher, which put a named livelihood on screen for the sake of a metaphor and also depended on an order that might not exist; its second version was folded into the class film in this group, where the object became a prop in somebody else's room. Pottery villages are a banned archetype on this slate and a sibling idea already works in clay, so this version keeps only the disc and the smoothing and takes them to a surface that people in this country already make by hand, for their own reasons, and that the source itself names.

concept_links.why: The film is this concept's first paragraph, filmed. The digest's own human reading of the practice begins as craft, and the sequence follows it step for step: picking out pebbles and twigs, working the earth level, and levelling it again each time it dries and cracks, until the face is as smooth as a drum skin [C087-P4:L209–L213]; then the instruction to hold one bare name and to ignore colour and texture, which the film narrates over a hand testing a finished surface [C087-P4:L213]; then the lay text's permission to build the object on a tray, a board or a patch of cement, which is the licence for the film to treat a working floor as the same kind of thing without claiming that it is one [C087-M:L19–L29]. Two of the digest's limits are spoken out loud rather than merely respected. The modest lay promise, half an hour to an hour a day over months for some steadiness and a blameless quieter life, is narrated in place of any claim that stillness fixes anything [C087-M:L13; C087-M:L39], and the admission that the full method is very hard and suits perhaps one in tens of thousands is narrated with it [C087-M:L9]. The supernormal powers listed as fruits of each device are named in the closing beat only in order to be refused as a promise, and no real person anywhere in the film is suggested to have any of them [C087-P4:L464–L484]. Every other limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured by construction: the film is not a stress-relief or productivity piece, because it ends on the source's own statement that calm is not what frees; it is not visualisation or manifesting, because the object is attended to by a bare name and the film shows no image and no light; it does not say 'withdraw from the world', because the work on screen is somebody's harvest; the mind-stream claim about rebirth is not used; and the traditional list of people said to be incapable of this practice is neither quoted, paraphrased nor implied, because the digest requires expert and sensitivity review before any use and because nothing in this film sorts anybody. The people making the floor are never presented as practising, and no attainment, calm or composure of theirs is claimed.

This concept gives the film its explanation and its brake, and one line of it gives the film its location. The digest's image for deep concentration is an ordinary act of attention: bringing a thing close, stopping looking anywhere else, and looking at its colours and marks for a long time until it is completely clear, which the film narrates over the finished empty floor rather than over any person [C013-P:L48–L52]. The digest names the earth disc as the standard object such attention is given to [C013-P:L155]. And the Pradeepika itself names a threshing floor as a place where somebody with long practice behind them may find the earth-device sign at once [C013-P:L133], which is why this film is on a threshing floor and not in a workshop: the source got there first, and the voice says so. The suppression limit is narrated in the source's own words, with the pot dipped into the pond and the moss drifting back, so that the film cannot be heard to say that a settled mind removes anything for good [C013-P:L62; C013-P:L66]. The digest's harder material is deliberately unused. 'Absorption is flow or being in the zone at work' is refused by construction, because the film never claims any state for the people working and never films a face to suggest one. The five higher knowledges are not narrated. And the sensitive passages about who cannot attain absorption, including the claims about people of certain rebirth types, the wealthy bound by greed and those guilty of grave deeds, are not quoted, not paraphrased and not alluded to, because the digest says they must never be used to judge anyone on screen and this film has real people in it.

This concept keeps the object in proportion and supplies the film's last sentence. The digest lists forty subjects and is strict that the object is matched to a person's temperament and taken from a teacher rather than picked by preference, which the film narrates at the moment the floor is buried under a crop and stops looking special [C085-P:L47]; and it states that the forty do not all reach the same depth, because ten of them bring the mind only as far as access and never into absorption [C085-P4:L61]. The digest's plainest correction, that settling is support and seeing is what frees, closes the film [C085-M:L11]. The digest's other limits are honoured. The film does not present any of this as mindfulness for stress relief. It does not say 'focus on whatever you like', because the fitting clause is spoken out loud. None of the corpse or food contemplations, the elements analysis, the butcher simile, the famine parable, the particle measures or the cosmology is used, and none is needed: this film takes one object out of the list and does not itemise the rest, which is also why it cannot become a lecture on the forty. The recollections and their restriction to noble disciples are not touched, and no rebirth benefit is offered to anybody.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the training in stillness these texts describe begins with a piece of ordinary craft rather than with a state of mind; that its first object is deliberately made dull, so that attention is asked to stay with something that gives it nothing; that the making is repetitive and has to be done again every time the surface cracks; that this is one of forty such supports, which are supposed to be fitted to the person and which do not all go the same distance; and that the sources themselves say a settled mind only holds things down while it lasts, and that what frees is a different piece of work. The floor is an analogy and the film says so. Nobody on screen is meditating, nobody's mind is visible, and nothing anybody here does is an attainment.
what_must_be_real: A floor that was going to be made anyway, made in its own order and at its own speed. No circle is prepared, re-plastered, swept, wetted or re-floated for the camera, no crack is opened or filled twice, nothing is carried in, and if the surface comes out badly or a shower puts it back, the film has that and keeps it. The people working are filmed as people doing work, are not named or followed as characters, are never described as meditating or as calm, and are not asked to confirm any doctrine or to hold still for a shot. No meditation object is brought to the location, nothing is placed on the floor that would not otherwise be on it, and no monk, teacher or practitioner is introduced into the frame to make the analogy for the film. The floor's own customs, including whatever is said or not said on it and by whom, belong to the people who use it and are not staged, invited or explained; nothing about them is presented as a spiritual practice or as evidence of anything. The holding whose floor and crop these are decides what is filmed, and no household's arrangements, earnings or yields are put on screen.
position_hint: opening the group, or very close to the opening: it is the plainest possible entry into the whole subject of the path, because it starts before any inner state, with somebody making a thing out of clay and sweeping the grit out of it. It also sets the group's guard rail on its first outing by ending on the source's own statement that calm is not what frees, which everything later in the group depends on. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting a working floor be heard as a meditation object, so that the film appears to claim that the people making it are practising, or that the object confers anything.
Turning the floor's own customs and the speech people keep on it into a spiritual set, which would make somebody's harvest into a ceremony for the camera.
Letting the traditional fruits of the practice, the powers listed further on in the source, be heard anywhere as a promise.
Overclaiming stillness as the answer, when both digests say calm holds things down only while it lasts and that seeing is what frees.
Making the work look picturesque or pre-modern, or turning the disappearance of hand threshing into a lament or into a verdict on people who use a machine.
Reciting the forty, or letting the film drift into a catalogue of meditation subjects.
Aestheticising the empty circle into a symbol of peace, when the film's claim is the opposite: it is a support that has to be made again every time it cracks.
Filming anybody's face in a way that invites the viewer to read a state of mind off it.
Putting a household's yield, debts or arrangements on screen because the floor happens to be where a crop is counted.
drop_if: Floors in this country are no longer made by hand with clay and dung, so the making, the cracking and the re-making, which are the film, cannot be filmed at all.
No holding will let its floor be prepared and used on camera on its own terms.
The only floors available are made for a camera, a heritage display or a festival rather than for a crop.
The harvest and the filming window cannot be made to meet, so the preparation would have to be staged.
Height cannot be obtained over the fields, so the one shot that states the concept, a plain disc in a landscape full of detail, is not available.

connections.note: One object made dull on purpose, against a whole range of prepared options standing ready for different people: the same list seen from one end and from the other.
This one makes the plain thing; the next is about what long, undistracted looking at one thing actually costs and commits you to.
From the groundwork of settling to the different work the sources say actually frees, which this film ends by pointing at and refusing to claim.

selection.reason: Its subject is the concept's own first paragraph filmed literally, on a surface the source itself names, and the most beautiful shot the place offers is a plain circle with nothing on it.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-24 into the footage-led shape, and relocated off a clay-worker's workshop. Two earlier passes are on the file: the first had a clay-worker making training discs to order for a meditation teacher, which depended on an order that might not exist and put a named livelihood on screen as a metaphor; the second folded the object into the lay-class film in this group, where it became a prop in a room full of real participants. Pottery villages are a banned archetype on this slate and a sibling idea in this group already works in clay, so this version keeps only what the brief allows, the disc and the smoothing, and takes them to a surface people in the dry zone make by hand for their own reasons: a threshing and drying floor, cleared of grit, plastered with termite-mound clay and cattle dung, floated flat, and floated flat again when it crazes. The decisive piece of research was in the C013 digest itself, which records that the Pradeepika names a threshing floor as a place where a practised person may find the earth-device sign at once [C013-P:L133]; the digest also carries this as a story seed. All three concepts were re-read from the digests as a new reader. Every citation was re-tested against digest evidence rather than copied from the old record: C013-P:L48–L52 is kept because it is the source's own image, but it is now narrated over an empty floor rather than over a person, and C085-P:L47 is kept because the digest does carry the fitting clause at that line. The closing beat states three refusals the group's floor requires: that nobody's calm is an attainment, that the listed powers are not a promise [C087-P4:L464–L484], and that calm is not what frees [C085-M:L11]. Nibbana is not mentioned, claimed or illustrated anywhere in this film, and no noble person, path moment or attainment appears. The sensitive Pradeepika passages about who cannot attain absorption are deliberately unused.

suggested_location.name: The hand-made threshing and drying floors of the tank villages of the Anamaduwa country, inland Puttalam District

also_known_as.name: kamatha
also_known_as.meaning: the threshing floor itself: a circle of beaten earth prepared beside the fields it serves, plastered and smoothed so that the crop does not pick up dust, grit or stones from the ground under it
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage across the paddy districts

also_known_as.name: vee gaha
also_known_as.meaning: the post set at the centre of the floor, around which cattle were driven to tread the crop out; often still standing where the treading itself has stopped

also_known_as.name: bolaththa
also_known_as.meaning: the twig besom used to sweep the cleared ground before the clay and dung go on, and to sweep the floor bare afterwards

also_known_as.name: kamatha basa
also_known_as.meaning: the separate set of words reported to be used on the floor in place of everyday ones; recorded in general accounts of the practice and not checked for this district

suggested_location.region: Puttalam District, North Western Province: the inland dry-zone interior in the east of the district, in the belt of small village tanks and tank-fed paddy well behind the lagoon and the coast road
suggested_location.why_here: Because the object the concept needs is a thing people in this country still make for themselves out of earth, and because this is the part of the island where it can be found away from both the coast and the wet zone. The interior of this district is dry-zone tank country: small reservoirs, paddy in the low ground, thorn scrub and coconut on the high ground, holdings of a few acres, and a divisional economy built on rice rather than on anything a camera has been to a hundred times. A floor here is made where the crop is, in the open, with a mammoty, a besom, a bucket of clay from a termite mound, cattle dung and water, and the standard it is finished to is exactly the standard in the text: no grit, no pebbles, no debris, nothing standing proud, and it is done again when it cracks. The setting also gives the film its one necessary shot, because a smooth pale disc lying in harvested strips, seen from height in low sun, is the plainest possible statement of an object made to have nothing about it. Nothing in the film is a household's private business: the floor is a work surface, the work is outdoors, nobody is asked about their inner life, and the doctrine stays with the voice. The district is thin on this slate, this part of it is thinner, and the country is quietly beautiful in a way that does not depend on a monument.
what_to_film: The finished floor from height in the first and last half hour, with the harvested strips, bunds and scrub around it, so the disc reads as a hole cut in a landscape full of detail; and the same frame at noon, when the shadows go and the circle almost disappears.

The clearing, at ground level and from a fixed position: weeds cut off with a mammoty without turning the soil under them, the besom going over the same ground repeatedly, and fingers lifting grit and pebbles out and dropping them into a tin.
The clay being dug from a termite mound and mixed with dung and water, and the slurry poured, spread and worked out with a wooden float and the heel of a hand.
The drying, filmed as two frames from the same position several hours apart, because it is the part of the work in which nothing appears to happen.
The crazed surface the next morning, close enough to count the cracks, then the same cracks filled with a thumb and the float going over them until its own marks stop showing.
A hand laid flat and drawn slowly across a finished face, and an eye held low along the surface to find a grain that should not be there.
The floor empty, held in one long still shot with nothing entering the frame, with the centre post standing in it.
The floor in use and unrecognisable: the crop spread across it, turned, raked and heaped, and then the floor swept bare again with dust and chaff going off the edge.
The tools put back, and the tin of picked-out grit tipped out at the edge of the field.
A floor that has been left, crazed and grown over at the edges, filmed in the same light as a working one, without commentary.
suggested_location.access: By road inland from the coast road and then on gravel and field tracks. Floors stand on private holdings beside the fields they serve, so everything depends on the holding whose floor and crop these are agreeing, approached through the divisional agrarian services office or a farmers' organisation the household already deals with rather than cold. There are no restricted-access, ordnance or protected-monument problems of the kind other parts of the island have; the practical constraints are the harvest calendar, the weather, and the fact that the work is done early and in heat. Drone flight over occupied holdings needs the holding's agreement whatever the general position is, and the low pass that makes the disc read has to be agreed in advance so that nothing is blown across a wet or a loaded floor. Nothing on the floor may be swept, wetted, re-floated or moved for the camera.
suggested_location.best_time: The harvest, and inside it the two or three days when a particular floor is being prepared, which is set by the crop rather than by a month. A dry, still stretch, because the surface is worked wet in the open and a shower puts it back to the beginning. Two visits are better than one: the making and the first cracking, then the day the crop comes onto it, which may be a week later. Within a day, first light and last light for the disc from height, and the middle of the day for the frame in which there is nothing to see.
suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the general accounts of the practice: the area is first cleared of weeds with a mammoty, taking care not to break the ground under them, and the debris swept off with a twig besom; a mix of clay taken from termite mounds and cattle dung is then applied densely to level the surface, and once dry it keeps the crop off the earth and free of dust and grit; a strong post is fixed at the centre, around which five or six cattle were driven to tread the crop out; and the floor carries its own customs, including a reported separate vocabulary used on it and restrictions on what may be eaten and said there. Three principal forms are described in the general literature, the commonest being laid directly on flat ground close to the fields. None of this material is specific to this district. The particular detail the film depends on most, that the surface crazes as it dries and is filled and floated again, is stated in the meditation source's own account of making a disc rather than in the agricultural accounts, which describe the plaster and the drying but not the repair; whether floors here are in practice re-plastered mid-season is unverified and is the first thing to check on the ground. The larger assumption is survival: threshing by cattle has largely been replaced by machines, and the same circle is now in many places prepared only for drying, so whether a floor in this district is still made by hand with clay and dung, and whether one will be made inside a filming window, is unknown. The coordinates are the published position of the inland divisional town at the centre of this paddy country and are a direction towards the country the film needs, not a survey: no floor, field, holding, household or farmers' organisation has been identified or approached, and no permission has been sought from anyone. No photograph of a hand-made threshing floor in this district, or of this work anywhere on the island, was found on Wikimedia Commons; searches returned scanned colonial-era books, a street and a clock tower in the divisional town, and a protected rock inscription nearby, none of which shows the floor, the paddy country or the work, so this record carries no image rather than an image of something else.

unknowns: Whether floors in this district are still made by hand with termite-mound clay and cattle dung, or whether the practice has gone over to cement, tarpaulins and mill yards.
Whether a floor is re-plastered and re-floated mid-season when it crazes, which is the beat the concept most needs.
When the harvest falls for any given holding here, and whether the two or three days of preparation can be made to meet a filming window.
Whether a holding will allow its floor and its crop to be filmed without the order or the timing of the work being adjusted.
Whether the customs kept on the floor can be left entirely alone on camera, and whether a household would rather they were not filmed at all.
Whether height can be obtained over these fields, and whether the disc reads from the air as strongly as it appears to from the ground.
Whether the reported separate vocabulary used on the floor is current in this district, and whether anyone would want it recorded.
